title: request-pipeline-cpu-smoke-profiles-wip
content:
Quick summary / goal:
This is a lightweight smoke-profiling log for CPU-side bottlenecks in the request pipeline. Focus areas: tokenization, request parsing/validation, thread pool handovers, and overall Python overhead (GIL + interpreter time). The goal is to identify low-effort mitigations we can ship in the next sprint that reduce median p99 request CPU time for small prompts (<256 tokens).

Context / why now:
- Recent customer reports of 40-60ms added tail latency for hosted text-gen routes on small inputs.
- Serving runtime shows GPU time is <10ms for model work (for these inputs) but host CPU time is the dominant contributor.
- Prior notes (see linked Confluence) touched tokenizers; we need a practical mitigation path.

Environment / stack sampled:
- Runtime: Python 3.12, Uvicorn + Gunicorn (uvloop worker class), FastAPI route handlers, RBAC middleware + JSON schema validation (pydantic v1.10).
- Tokenizer: two variants used in experiments: sentencepiece-python (C++/Python bindings) and transformers Tokenizers (Rust via huggingface-tokenizers).
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, 8 vCPU, single GPU.
- Workload: synthetic replay of production traces (2000 requests, median prompt length 32 tokens, mean 48).

Tools / commands used:
- py-spy record -o flame.svg --native -p <pid> --duration 30
- python -m cProfile -o /tmp/profile.out runners/fastpath_smoke.py
- perf record -g -p <pid> -- sleep 30; perf script | flamegraph.pl > perf-flame.svg
- small microbench harness using timeit + multiprocessing to simulate thread pool behavior

High-level findings (smoke numbers):
- Total added CPU per request (median): ~18.6ms
  - Tokenization (sentencepiece-python): 7.8ms
  - JSON parsing & request validation: 3.1ms
  - Middleware/metrics extraction (tagging, trace context): 1.4ms
  - Thread pool handoff / executor.submit + result retrieval: 2.7ms
  - Python interpreter overhead (call stacks, coroutine scheduling): 3.6ms

Notes on tokenizers:
- sentencepiece-python (current safe default) is fast for large batches but has ~8ms per-request latency on small prompts (observed). The hot path sits in Python C-extension with noticeable GIL holds.
- huggingface/tokenizers (Rust + PyO3 wrapper) runs at ~0.7ms per request with the same input — ~10x faster in our microbench. The migration delta is large; however, compatibility/normalization differences (e.g., pretokenization rules) need validation.
- Observed that for the sentencepiece binding the GIL is held for the entire encode call; py-spy shows ~95% of the time in the tokenizer C-extension when it's active.

Request parsing & validation:
- pydantic v1-based validation costs about 3ms on average due to recursive model construction for nested request shapes.
- Fast-path requests (simple text-gen) still go through full validation; we can gate a lightweight schema for short inputs: earlier trampoline that does a quick type check in ~0.4ms and only runs full pydantic validation for complex shapes.

Thread pool behavior:
- We use a small ThreadPoolExecutor to offload blocking tokenization in places where the tokenizer cannot be made async-native. Context switch + task scheduling overhead is ~2.5ms per offload in our config (submit + future.result()).
- Continuous batching interactions: when requests land close together, offloading to threads increases variability due to worker queueing; observed tail spikes when CPU contention hits ~6 cores.
- Per-core run queue traces show many short-lived threads waking frequently; switching to a shared process pool (multiprocessing) with long-lived workers reduces per-call overhead but increases memory footprint and complexity (pickle costs).

Python overhead / GIL observations:
- Even when using Rust tokenizer, overall Python-layer time was ~4-5ms: await scheduling, middleware, JSON serialization, and small utility functions (signature creation, metrics).
- Profiling shows frequent short-lived allocations and small vector/list constructions in request pipeline — not catastrophic, but measurable at p99.
- Some hot functions: Request.build_signature (0.7ms), metrics.increment_token_count (0.5ms), route_dispatch (0.9ms).

Sample flamegraph observations:
- Biggest single box when using sentencepiece: tokenizer.encode -> CPython C-extension
- With Rust tokenizer: the largest boxes are framework CRCs (uvloop callbacks) and route_dispatch/validation

Microbench experiments (commands + outputs):
1) Tokenizer microbench (avg of 500 runs):
   - sentencepiece: mean 7.82ms, p95 12.0ms
   - hf-tokenizers (rust): mean 0.72ms, p95 1.3ms
2) Request validation fallback:
   - full pydantic validation: mean 3.2ms
   - lightweight guard + conditional validate: mean 0.42ms for guarded requests
3) Thread offload pattern:
   - inline tokenization (same process): median 0.9ms additional scheduling cost when using Rust tokenizer
   - threadpool offload (sentencepiece): median +2.7ms overhead

Immediate mitigation candidates (low friction):
- Swap default tokenizer to huggingface/tokenizers for hosted routes where model tokenization rules match. Start with an A/B experiment on 10% traffic. (effort: small PR + validation tests)
- Implement a short-circuit lightweight request guard: for simple text-gen shapes bypass full pydantic and do minimal checks (types + length). (effort: tiny, high ROI)
- Stop offloading to ThreadPool when using Rust tokenizers; keep tokenization inline (async-friendly). This reduces context switch overhead. (effort: small config change)
- Add a pooled process worker for legacy sentencepiece tasks as a mid-term (if migration infeasible). Use keep-alive workers to avoid per-call spawn costs. (effort: medium)

Longer-term / higher effort changes:
- Move critical path to C-extension or Rust shim for route serialization/metrics incrementers. Consider PyO3 for small hot helpers. (effort: medium+)
- Re-evaluate pydantic v2 or custom fast validators for request shapes — v2 shows promise in synthetic tests for lower allocation overhead. (effort: medium)
- Profile GC pauses under load; consider generational tuning for high-throughput servers.

Open questions / experiments to run next:
- Are tokenization differences between tokenizers affecting model outputs enough to fail customer tests? Need automatic metrics to compare token-level diffs across representative prompts. (next: run 500-k prompt diff script)
- Cost/benefit for replacing pydantic with a minimal C extension for our canonical route shapes. (next: spike prototype for one route)
- Does adding a tiny CachingLayer for recent prefix tokenizations (shared LRU) reduce repeated cost for common short system prompts? Memory vs hit-rate tradeoff needs simulation.

Quick action items (owner: Rina unless noted):
- [ ] PR: implement lightweight request guard, add tests (due 2026-03-16)
- [ ] Experiment: rollout hf-tokenizers on hosted small-gen routes (10% traffic) and collect tokenization diffs + latency delta (owner: Mateo)
- [ ] Add py-spy smoke harness to CI for nightly p99 regressions (owner: Jinsoo)
- [ ] Spike: pooled process worker for sentencepiece fallback (owner: Hannah)

Rough risk matrix:
- Replace tokenizer default: high latency improvement, medium risk if tokenization outputs differ. Must gate by automated token-diff tests and one canary region.
- Shortcut validation: low risk, high gain (should add thorough tests to avoid malformed requests).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally experimental and contains microbench numbers from short runs. Numbers should be validated in a larger-scale canary before sweeping changes.
- If you have a previous perf harness for tokenization that we can re-use, add link here and tag me.

End of notes.

Unresolved fragments / TODO (scratchpad):
- collect 1k-case with varying prompt lengths (8, 32, 128, 512) to map cost curve
- try switching off pydantic for route-dispatch in a non-prod branch and measure errors vs payloads seen in logs
- check memory impact of process pool workers (estimate 120MB/w worker for sentencepiece binary)
